holidays.name: Four Prunes Day
holidays.description: A day for snacking on dried plums. The name comes from the idea that eating about four to nine prunes in one sitting can keep your digestion running smoothly. Treat yourself to prunes in oatmeal, stuffed with cheese, or straight from the bag.
holidays.origin: This is an unofficial observance. It is named after the old advice that a handful of prunes helps with digestive regularity. Plum growers later rebranded prunes as 'dried plums' to shake off their reputation as a laxative fruit.
holidays.funFact: Prunes are plums that have been dried, and they shrink to about a third of their fresh size. Their reputation as a gentle digestive aid is so strong that sellers have started calling them 'dried plums' to improve their image.

holidays.name: National Mulligan Day
holidays.description: A day of second chances. Take a do-over on a botched golf shot, a bad haircut, a burnt dinner, or a awkward email. Forgive yourself and anyone else who needs a fresh start.
holidays.origin: It is an unofficial observance that borrows its name from the golf 'mulligan', a friendly free replay of a bad shot. The exact origin of the day is unclear.
holidays.funFact: Nobody is sure where the word 'mulligan' in golf comes from. One popular story credits a Canadian locker-room golfer named Mulligan from the 1920s, though the tale has never been firmly proven.

holidays.name: National Pasta Day
holidays.description: A carb-loaded celebration of spaghetti, penne, rigatoni, and every other noodle shape. It's a good excuse to twirl, slurp, and drown something in sauce.
holidays.origin: This is an unofficial food holiday, popular with restaurants and home cooks. It has no clear single founder.
holidays.funFact: Italy makes hundreds of pasta shapes, and many have wonderfully odd names. Strozzapreti means 'priest stranglers', and orecchiette means 'little ears'.
